headings.title: Anatomical Overview and Gross Structure
headings.content: The cerebellum, often called the "little brain," sits at the base of the skull in the posterior cranial fossa, just beneath the occipital lobes of the cerebrum. Separated from the cerebral cortex by the tentorium cerebelli, it contains over half of all the neurons in the entire central nervous system despite its compact size. Grossly, the organ consists of two lateral hemispheres joined in the midline by a narrow strip called the vermis. Transverse fissures divide the surface into distinct lobes: the anterior lobe, the posterior lobe, and the tiny flocculonodular lobe, which represents the oldest evolutionary part of the structure. Three pairs of large nerve fiber bundles, known as the cerebellar peduncles, anchor the cerebellum to the brainstem. These superior, middle, and inferior peduncles form the sole anatomical highways for all incoming and outgoing communication between the cerebellum and the rest of the nervous system.

headings.title: Microscopic Architecture of the Cortex
headings.content:
A cross-section through the cerebellar cortex reveals a uniform, highly folded three-layered sheet of gray matter. 

- **Molecular layer**: The outermost zone, containing mostly unmyelinated granule cell axons (parallel fibers), dendritic trees of Purkinje cells, and inhibitory interneurons like basket and stellate cells.
- **Purkinje cell layer**: A single monolayer of massive, flask-shaped neuronal cell bodies that represent the sole output channel of the entire cerebellar cortex.
- **Granule cell layer**: The deepest, densely packed layer made of millions of tiny granule cells whose axons ascend to the molecular layer and synapse on Purkinje dendrites.

headings.title: Functional Divisions and Circuitry
headings.content:
Functionally, the cerebellum divides into three distinct zones, each linked to specific neural circuits:

1. **Vestibulocerebellum (Archicerebellum)**: Consists mainly of the flocculonodular lobe, receiving vestibular input to control balance, posture, and eye movements.
2. **Spinocerebellum (Paleocerebellum)**: Comprises the vermis and intermediate zones, receiving proprioceptive input from the spinal cord to regulate muscle tone and ongoing body movements.
3. **Cerebrocerebellum (Neocerebellum)**: Formed by the lateral hemispheres, communicating extensively with the cerebral cortex to plan and time complex, skilled movements.

All cortical output funnels through four pairs of deep cerebellar nuclei embedded in the white matter: the dentate, emboliform, globose, and fastigial nuclei. These deep nuclei fire spontaneous action potentials that are continuously shaped by inhibitory signals from Purkinje cells.

headings.title: Physiological Roles in Motor Control
headings.content: Rather than initiating voluntary movement, the cerebellum acts as a high-speed error-correcting computer. It compares the intended motor plan coming from the motor cortex with sensory feedback arriving from active muscles and joints. If a discrepancy occurs, the cerebellum rapidly adjusts motor output via pathways looping through the thalamus and brainstem. This ongoing comparison ensures smooth, precise movements without tremor, overshoot, or clumsiness. It also plays a critical role in motor learning, such as riding a bicycle or playing a musical instrument, where repetition refines the internal models stored within the cerebellar circuits.

headings.title: Clinical Correlates and Signs of Dysfunction
headings.content: Damage to the cerebellum or its connecting pathways produces a characteristic set of motor deficits, generally grouped under the term ataxia. Unlike paralysis, cerebellar lesions do not weaken muscles, but they destroy coordination, rhythm, and accuracy. Common clinical signs include intention tremor (shaking that worsens as the hand approaches a target), dysdiadochokinesia (inability to perform rapid alternating movements like pronation and supination), and dysmetria (overshooting or undershooting a target during point-to-point testing). Patients may also display a wide-based, unsteady staggering gait resembling alcohol intoxication, alongside slurred, scanning speech patterns.
